list.listitem: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder with high penetrance characterized by parathyroid hyperplasia/adenomas, enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and pituitary adenomas. Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is the most common, followed by enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and pituitary adenomas. B
The onset of these tumors is insidious and their progression is usually slow; this may have a bearing on the time and type of diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. B
Diagnosis of these tumors generally follows the diagnostic approach in the sporadic types. B

The management is more complex and should be individualized. It includes subtotal parathyroidectomy for PHPT and medical or surgical therapy for enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and pituitary tumors. B

background.definition: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an autosomal dominant familial neoplasia syndrome characterized mainly by parathyroid hyperplasia/adenomas, pituitary adenomas, and enteropancreatic endocrine tumors. Other tumors associated with MEN1 include thymic carcinoids, thymoma, bronchial carcinoids, functional and nonfunctional adrenal tumors, lipomas, facial angiofibromas, collagenomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas.

list.listitem: MEN1 is a familial hereditary syndrome. First degree relatives have a 50% risk of developing the disease.
Based on postmortem studies, the incidence of MEN1 is estimated to be about 0.25% and the prevalence 0.02 to 0.2 per 1000.
MEN1 is caused by germline mutations in a tumor suppressor gene located on the long arm of chromosome 11(11q13) that encodes a 610-amino acid protein named menin.
Menin is a nuclear protein involved in transcriptional regulation and cell proliferation.
In MEN1, inactivating mutations in the MEN1 gene leads to loss of the tumor suppressor effect of menin.
It is presumed that affected patients are born with a germline mutation in one allele of the MEN1 gene (first hit).
An acquired somatic mutation in the other allele in the affected tissue (second hit) leads to loss of the tumor suppressor function of menin with consequent hyperplastic and adenomatous change.
There is no clear genotype/phenotype correlation.
The value of screening for MEN1 gene mutations is questionable since there is no clear genotype/phenotype correlation and the tumors in MEN1 are generally slow growing and benign. B

MEN1 mutation detection, however, can be of significant help in cases with features suggestive of MEN1 such as an index case in which the patient meets the clinical criteria of MEN1 without a family history (see definition) or in an asymptomatic member of a family with known mutation MEN1 syndrome. C
Based on expert opinion and the high prevalence of these tumors in MEN1, MEN1 carriers should be screened regularly for gastrinoma, insulinoma, and other tumors.C

In MEN1 mutation carriers who do not manifest the disease or have only some features of the disease, a consensus guideline recommended screening as follows:
For primary hyperparathyroidism: screening should start at age 8 years with annual measurement of calcium and parathyroid hormone. For gastropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (NET): start at age 20 years with an annual measurement of gastrin, glucagon, vasointestinal polypeptide, pancreatic polypeptide, chromogranin A, and insulin with a fasting glucose. While imaging may depend on local resources, a minimal protocol includes annual pancreatic and duodenal imaging with MRI, CT or endoscopic ultrasound. For thymic, bronchopulmonary, and gastric NET: chromogranin A and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid are not recommended. CT or MRI of the chest every 1 to 2 years to look for thymic and lung NET is recommended. Gastroscopy with biopsy every 3 years is recommended for MEN1 patients with elevated gastrin levels. For insulinoma: start screening at age 5 years with fasting glucose and insulin annually. For pituitary tumors: start at age 5 years with measurement of prolactin and Insulin-like growth factor-1 annually and MRI every 3 to 5 years. For adrenal tumors: CT or MRI every 3 years.

A consensus guideline for patients with MEN1 suggests: the following screening tests for different tumors:
Insulinoma: Annual fasting glucose and insuling starting at age 5 years. Other pancreatic neuroendocrine syndromes: Annual chromogranin-A, pancreatic polypeptide, glucagon, VIP; annual MRI, CT or endoscopic ultrasound starting no later than age 10 years Gastrinoma: Annual serum gastrin +/- gastric pH starting at age 20 years

MEN1 syndrome should be suspected when 2 of the 3 classical components of MEN1 are present or when there is a family history of MEN1 or MEN1-associated mutation in the presence of one or more typical or atypical features of MEN1. B
Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is usually the first manifestation and is diagnosed when there is hypercalcemia with elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone. B

Gastrinoma is the most common enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor; diagnosis is based on high gastrin level in the presence of low gastric fluid pH of less than 5 or an abnormal serum gastrin in the secretin-stimulation test. B
Pituitary adenomas occur in about 40%, most commonly prolactinomas and growth hormone secreting tumors causing acromegaly. B
The 3 cardinal features of MEN 1 are: Primary hyperparathyroidism due to parathyroid hyperplasia (>90%). Enteropancreatic endocrine tumors (~60%). Pituitary adenomas (~40%).
The classical components of MEN1 are primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and pituitary adenomas.
See chapters on hyperparathyroidism and insulinoma for typical clinical presentation.

Gastrinomas are usually associated with significant gastric hyperacidity, severe heartburn, epigastric pain, and multiple recurrent peptic ulcer disease. Patients may also complain of chronic diarrhea.

Nonfunctional enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may present with vague upper abdominal pain or symptoms related to pressure on adjacent structures such as jaundice from pressure on biliary ducts.

Glucagonomas presenting with abdominal pain, anemia, hyperglycemia, and characteristic skin lesions (necrolytic migratory erythema) or vasoactive intestinal polypeptide-secreting tumor (VIPoma) presenting with secretory diarrhea rarely occur in MEN1.

Pituitary tumors are frequently associated with high prolactin (prolactinoma). They may present with irregular menses and galactorrhea in females or secondary hypogonadism with erectile dysfunction and gynecomastia in males. Patients with acromegaly may complain of increased sweating, snoring, changes in the size of hands and feet, and coarse facial features.

Characteristic skin tumors are common and can be useful clues to the diagnosis of MEN1 in the right context. These include facial angiofibromas, acneiform papules on the face and around the lips; collagenomas, skin-colored cutaneous nodules usually on the trunk or neck; and lipomas found anywhere in the body.
See chapter on hyperparathyroidism for diagnosis of this condition. Localizing techniques are generally not needed for PHPT in MEN1, as surgery entails 4-gland exploration.

For gastrinomas: serum gastrin greater than 1000 pg/mL in the presence of acidic gastric fluids (pH <5 of a random gastric fluid specimen) is usually diagnostic. A secretin-stimulation test might be indicated in lesser degrees of elevation of serum gastrin; rapid infusion of secretin 0.4 mcg/kg over 1 minute causes significant elevation of gastrin (>200 pg/mL) about 10 minutes later in gastrinomas. Discontinuation of proton pump inhibitors can lead to adverse events and should be done cautiously.

See chapter on insulinoma for diagnosis of this condition. CT scan of the pancreas and upper abdomen, MRI, 111-indium-labeled octreotide scan, and endoscopic ultrasonography are imaging techniques that are used to localize the site of the tumor(s).

If pituitary tumor is suspected, measure serum prolactin and insulin-like growth factor 1 and consider a glucose tolerance test with serial measurements of growth hormone when acromegaly is suspected. MRI is the standard imaging technique for the patient with suspected pituitary tumor.

Suspect MEN1 syndrome when 2 of the 3 classical components of MEN1 (PHPT, enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, or pituitary adenoma) are present or when there is a family history of MEN1 or MEN1-associated mutation in the presence of one or more typical or atypical features of MEN1.

PHPT is usually the first manifestation and is present in more than 90% of patients by age 40. Enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors occur in about 60% of patients, and gastrinoma is the most common; pituitary adenomas occur in about 40%, and prolactinomas are the most common.

The diagnosis of PHPT is suggested by hypercalcemia; gastrinoma is suggested by the presence of symptoms of gastric hyperacidity and elevated serum gastrin; and insulinoma is suggested by elevated or normal insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide in the presence of hypoglycemia.
Treatment should ideally be in a center with extensive experience with diagnosis and treatment of MEN1. C
Surgery is the primary therapeutic modality for PHPT and enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. However, its timing and indications are controversial and complex.B
Medical management of gastrinomas using proton pump inhibitors is very effective; the indication and type of surgery for removal of the tumor should be individualized. B

Surgery is indicated for insulinomas; for other enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, somatostatin analogs are usually effective in controlling hormonal hypersecretion, but surgery remains a primary option for large tumors or those with pressure effect. B

For inoperable or metastatic enteropancreatic tumors, somatostatin analogs, alpha-interferon, radiolabeled octreotide therapy, embolization or chemoembolization, systemic chemotherapy, and palliative surgery may provide variable palliative benefits.
Pituitary tumors in MEN1 are managed in a similar way to sporadic tumors. C
See chapters on hyperparathyroidism and insulinoma for a more detailed discussion of treatment of those conditions.

For gastrinomas, medical management with proton pump inhibitors (eg, omeprazole 20-40 mg a day) is very effective in controlling symptoms related to the high gastric acid output. However, surgery is recommended for patients with a high likelihood of malignancy and metastases (tumors >3 cm or those associated with lymphadenopathy) or in cases of local pressure effects.
Apart from insulinomas, symptoms related to hormonal hypersecretion of most entero-pancreatic tumors respond to somatostatin analogs (eg, long-acting octreotide 20-30 mg IM q 28 days).
For prolactinomas, dopamine receptor agonists are the treatment of choice (eg, cabergoline 0.25-1 mg twice/week).
Other pituitary tumors are treated in the same way as in sporadic tumors.

See chapter on hyperparathyroidism for recommendations regarding surgical management. Near-total parathyroidectomy is the classical surgery for PHPT in MEN1. This is usually achieved by removal of three and a half of the most abnormal-looking parathyroid glands, with preservation of one-half of the most normal-looking gland. Total thymectomy is done at the same time to prevent future development of thymic carcinoids.
Total thymectomy should be performed with parathyroidectomy to prevent future development of thymic carcinoids.

The indications for surgery are similar to those for sporadic PHPT; these include symptoms or evidence of end-organ damage. In addition, in cases of PHPT and gastrinoma, early parathyroidectomy is indicated, as it may substantially decrease gastrin level.

A meta-analysis identified 21 cohort studies with 1131 patients comparing total parathyroidectomy (n=272), subtotal parathyroidectomy (n=510), and less than subtotal (n=349). The risk of long term hypoparathyroidism was greater with total parathyroidectomy than with subtotal (RR 1.6, 95% CI 1.1 - 2.3). However, the risk of recurrence (RR 1.4), persistent hyperparathyroidism (RR 2.3) and reoperation for hyperparathyroidism (RR 2.5) were higher with subtotal or less than subtotal resection.
A randomized trial compared subtotal parathyroidectomy with total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation in 32 patients with MEN type 1 parathyroid disease. There was no difference in outcomes.

The timing of surgery is controversial for asymptomatic PHPT in MEN1; early parathyroidectomy may decrease the exposure to the effects of parathyroid hormone, while late surgery might be simpler and associated with less risk of recurrence.
For enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, the tumors are frequently multiple and the indication and timing of surgery are more complex.
In general, tumors larger than 3 cm carry a significant risk of metastases, and surgery might be indicated.
For patients with MEN1 pancreatic endocrine tumors, major pancreatic resection provides a lower risk of recurrence but a higher risk of post-operative endocrine insufficiency.
For pituitary tumors other than prolactinomas, the indications for surgery in MEN1 are similar to those of sporadic pituitary tumors.
For patients with recurrent hypercalcemia after surgery, a case series at the Mayo Clinic concluded that percutaneous ethanol ablation was a safe and effective treatment.

For inoperable or metastatic enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, somatostatin analogs, alpha-interferon, radiolabeled octreotide therapy, embolization or chemoembolization, systemic chemotherapy, and palliative surgery may provide variable palliative benefits.
The prognosis of MEN1 is generally good. B
It depends to a great extent on the behavior of enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, especially in the presence of distant metastases. B
Screening and early intervention may improve long-term outcome but is not well studied. C

Neuroendocrine tumors of thymus occurred in 3.4% of patients in a large Dutch registry, but have high mortality (10 year survival 25%). Neuroendocrine tumors of lung occurred in 13%, and had better survival (10 year survival 71%).
For primary hyperparathyroidism: screening should start at age 8 years with annual measurement of calcium and parathyroid hormone.

For gastropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (NET): start at age 20 years with an annual measurement of gastrin, glucagon, vasointestinal polypeptide, pancreatic polypeptide, chromogranin A, and insulin with a fasting glucose. While imaging may depend on local resources, a minimal protocol includes annual pancreatic and duodenal imaging with MRI, CT or endoscopic ultrasound.

A study comparing (68)Gallium-DOTATATE PET/CT with (111)In-pentetreotide SPECT/CT and anatomic imaging with CT scan in 26 patients with MEN Type 1 found that the former was more sensitive (107 lesions detected versus 33 and 48, respectively, using the other methods). A change in management resulted for 8 of the 26 patients as a result.

For thymic, bronchopulmonary, and gastric NET: chromogranin A and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid are not recommended. CT or MRI of the chest every 1 to 2 years to look for thymic and lung NET is recommended. Gastroscopy with biopsy every 3 years is recommended for MEN1 patients with elevated gastrin levels.
For insulinoma: start screening at age 5 years with fasting glucose and insulin annually.
For pituitary tumors: start at age 5 years with measurement of prolactin and Insulin-like growth factor-1 annually and MRI every 3 to 5 years.
For adrenal tumors: CT or MRI every 3 years.

A retrospective cohort study identify 160 patients with MEN type 1 with onset of symptoms before 21 years of age. The most common initial symptoms were those caused hyperparathyroidism (75%), pituitary adenoma (34%), insulinoma (12%), and non-secreting pancreating tumor (9%). Symptoms beginning before age 10 years were uncommon (14% of patients).
In this cohort, 41% had surgery during childhood or adolescence, largely for hyperparathyroidism or gastrinoma. Four patients had malignant lesions and one died before age 21 years.
